newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia revamps ruble, says inflation beaten.
newsitem.headline: Russia revamps ruble, says inflation beaten.

text.p: Russia announced Monday that it would slash three zeroes from the face values of the ruble currency from the start of next year in a redenomination that President Boris Yeltsin promised would not hurt the public.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais supported the move, saying Russia had studied examples of currency reforms in other countries like Ukraine and Poland, and chosen what it considered to be the least disruptive step.

"Inflationary financing, stabilisation, redenomination; this is the triad through which dozens of countries have passed, some with great difficulty and others with less," Chubais said. "The redenomination (in Russia) was chosen as the most gentle way."
He said the government hoped to avoid the bitter experience of Soviet times, when monetary reform led to panic among the population and people's life savings becoming worthless paper overnight.

Yeltsin said Russians would not have to exchange old notes for new ones, and would be able to use the old denomination until the end of the year. The central bank would continue to exchange old money for new until the end of 2002.
"In the last 50 years, everything connected with monetary reform always hit ordinary people here. Now that is ruled out. As president, I guarantee this," Yeltsin said.
Central bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin said the move meant hyperinflation and economic stagnation was over, and that Russia had embarked on the path to economic growth and a strong ruble.

"All necessary conditions for transferring to economic growth in Russia are established," he said. "We hope the new heavy, firm ruble will firm in the future and its inflationary depreciation will slow down even more than this year."
Consumer prices rose just 14.5 percent year-on-year in June, down from over a 1,000 percent climb in late 1993. The government forecasts inflation of just 3 percent in 2000.
Dubinin said the central bank would not change its currency policy as a result of the redenomination.
"For foreign investors this move is fairly neutral but in the bigger picture it's a tangible sign of Russia's success in reducing inflation," said David Boren, economist at Salomon Bros. in London.

Since 1995, the central bank has been holding the ruble in a wide currency band, setting target rates for the start and the end of the year and allowing the ruble to depreciate gently in line with inflation. The ruble barely reacted to the news, ending the day where it had started at about 5,800 per dollar.
A key aim of the currency reform was to accelerate the "de-dollarization" of the Russian economy.
"The level of currency reserves does not worry me. What worries me much more is the share of the population's savings being spent on buying hard currency," Chubais said.
"It has been high, it is high, and by all accounts it will be high, and that is not good ... For the economy this is bad, because we are funding the U.S. government," he told reporters.

The authoritative Izvestiya daily said in its Tuesday edition that nearly 21 percent of all Russians' earnings were spent on hard currency in the first half of 1997, up from 16.3 in the first six months of last year.
Yeltsin also sought to reassure Russians that keeping accounts in the new "super-ruble" was safe.
"Once you receive your wages, it is no longer necessary today, as it was not long ago, to run to the exchange kiosk. You can keep your bank savings in ruble accounts," Yeltsin said.

Another reason for doing away with "superfluous" zeroes was purely practical. Calculations are done in millions, billions and even trillions of rubles, causing headaches for everyone from oil firms to old age pensioners.
The ruble reforms will mean that one new ruble will be worth 1,000 old ones, or 17 cents at current rates. The U.S. dollar is currently equal to 5,800 rubles.
Analysts said the net impact of the move will be felt internally by making big-ticket transactions less unwieldy in rubles, rendering the use of dollars for these purposes less attractive.
The biggest ruble note in circulation at present is 500,000, or about $86.
Western economists welcomed the move, agreeing it was a sign of growing price stability in post-Soviet Russia.

"It's certainly an encouraging sign of the government's confidence in its ability to maintain low inflation," said Martin Gilman, International Monetary Fund representative in Moscow. "It's more symbolic ... In terms of economic fundamentals it doesn't change anything," he added.
Chubais did not rule out the possibility of inflation quickening as a result of the ruble redenomination. But it would only be for the short term and limited in scale, he added.
He said the government was expecting a monthly rate of 0.5-0.6 percent in August, but the reform, starting in January, could push the rate a few tenths of a point higher.
